# maiman

The public surface is deliberately small: if a feature is not reachable from here, it does not exist. Generated from the docstrings.

## Building and running a graph

### `maiman.SimulationContext`

```python
class SimulationContext(bit_rate: float, samples_per_symbol: int, sequence_length: int, seed: int = 0, precision: Precision = single) -> None
```

Parameters that every component in a run must agree on.

Sample rate, sample count and time origin belong to the *run*, not to
individual signals. If each signal carried its own, two blocks could
silently disagree about the time window and the simulation would be
meaningless while still producing plausible-looking numbers.

- `complex_dtype` — NumPy dtype for sampled complex fields.
- `num_samples` — N, the number of samples in the time window.
- `real_dtype` — NumPy dtype for sampled real waveforms.
- `rng` — A generator derived deterministically from the seed and `key`.
- `sample_rate` — Fs [Hz].
- `time_axis` — Sample times [s], starting at zero.
- `time_step` — dt [s].
- `time_window` — T [s], the total simulated duration.

### `maiman.Graph`

```python
class Graph(ctx: SimulationContext) -> None
```

A directed graph of components, executed by `run`.

- `add` — Add a component and return it, so it can be assigned in one line.
- `chain` — Connect a sequence of single-input/single-output components in order.
- `connect` — Wire an output port to an input port.
- `edges` — Connections, keyed by the destination `(label, port name)`.
- `run` — Execute every component once, in dependency order.

### `maiman.Results`

```python
class Results(values: dict[tuple[str, str], Signal]) -> None
```

Signals produced by a run, addressed by component and port.

- `items` — Every retained result, as `((label, port name), signal)` pairs.
- `port` — The signal on one named output port.

### `maiman.sweep`

```python
sweep(graph: Graph, axes: Mapping[AxisKey, Sequence[float | bool]], *, runs: int = 1, keep: list[Component] | None = None, fixed: Mapping[AxisKey, float | bool] | None = None, workers: int | None = 1) -> SweepResult
```

Run `graph` once for every combination of the given parameter values.

`axes` maps `(component, parameter)` to the values it should take; the
sweep covers their cartesian product, varying the last axis fastest.

`runs` repeats each point with independently derived seeds. That is what
turns a noisy measurement into a distribution — a single BER estimate at a
marginal operating point is one sample, not an answer.

`fixed` applies the same override at every point, which saves editing the
graph just to hold something constant for one study.

`workers` runs that many points at a time, each on its own deep copy of the
graph; `None` picks one per core, capped at the number of points. The
default of 1 is sequential and copies nothing, because a sweep of four cheap
points is slower to parallelise than to run.

**The answer does not depend on it.** Every point is a function of its own
overrides and its own derived seed, so the numbers are identical however many
workers ran them, and they come back in sweep order regardless of the order
they finished in. There is a test on exactly that.

The graph is left exactly as it was found, including if a run raises — and
above one worker it is never run at all, only copied.

### `maiman.SweepResult`

```python
class SweepResult(points: tuple[SweepPoint, ...], axes: dict[str, tuple[float | bool, ...]]) -> None
```

Every point of a sweep, in the order the axes were given.

- `axis` — The values one axis took, in sweep order.
- `metric` — Pull one number out of every run, shaped `(points, runs)`.

### `maiman.SweepPoint`

```python
class SweepPoint(index: int, values: dict[str, float | bool], runs: tuple[Results, ...]) -> None
```

One combination of swept parameter values, with the runs taken there.

## The component model

### `maiman.Component`

```python
class Component(*, label: str | None = None, **params: float | bool) -> None
```

Base class for every block in a simulation graph.

A component is a pure function of its inputs and its parameters: it receives
read-only signals and returns new ones. Nothing is mutated in place, so the
scheduler is free to order, cache, or parallelise execution. The single
exception is a loop control, which carries one pass's input into the next;
see `feedback_passes`.

- `check_port_groups` — Refuse groups that do not describe this component's ports.
- `display` — The value of parameter `name` in its declared unit, with the unit.
- `feedback_passes` — How many passes a loop closed through this block runs; 0 if it closes none.
- `manifest` — The component description consumed by the GUI.
- `param_specs` — Every `Param` declared on this class or a base class.
- `port_groups` — Independent slices of this component, for the scheduler.
- `report` — Say how far through this component's own work the run has got, 0 to 1.
- `reset_feedback` — Forget whatever was carried between passes. Called at the start of every run.
- `run` — Process the whole time window and return one signal per output port.
- `si` — The value of parameter `name` converted to its SI base unit.
- `sole_input` — The only input port, for chaining. Raises if there is not exactly one.
- `sole_output` — The only signal-carrying output port, for chaining.
- `structural_config` — Constructor arguments that are not parameters.
- `type_name` — The name this component is stored under in project files.
- `validate` — Refuse a combination of this component's own parameters.

### `maiman.Param`

```python
class Param(default: float, *, unit: str = , min: float | None = None, max: float | None = None, choices: Sequence[float] | None = None, doc: str = , applies_when: str | None = None) -> None
```

A component parameter, declared once, with its unit and valid values.

The unit is part of the declaration rather than a comment, so that
`Component.si` can convert consistently and the GUI manifest can be
generated from the same source. Declaring parameters twice — once in code
and once in a manifest file — guarantees they drift apart.

`min`/`max` bound a continuous quantity. `choices` is for the other
kind: a parameter whose legal values are a *set*, not an interval. A PRBS
order may be 7, 9, 11, 15, 23 or 31 and nothing between; a QAM format is 1,
2, 4, 6 or 8 bits per symbol and never 3. Declaring those as a range was a
quiet lie — the field said "1 … 8", the editor accepted 3, and only the
engine knew that 8-QAM is a cross constellation nobody has implemented. An
interface can offer a set as a list to choose from and cannot offer an
interval as anything but a box to type in, so the distinction earns its
keep on screen as well as in validation.

`applies_when` names a `BoolParam` on the same component that this
parameter only takes effect under — `"saturate"`, or `"!auto_span"` for
one that applies when the flag is *off*. It changes nothing about how the
parameter behaves; what it does is let an interface grey out a box that
cannot do anything, instead of offering a control that is quietly ignored.

It lives here rather than in the interface for the reason every other part of
a manifest does: the condition is a fact about the model, the code that reads
the parameter is three files away from the code that draws the box, and a
table of these maintained beside the editor is a table that goes stale the
first time a flag is renamed.

- `to_dict` — The JSON-serialisable description used to generate GUI manifests.

### `maiman.BoolParam`

```python
class BoolParam(default: bool, *, doc: str = , applies_when: str | None = None) -> None
```

A component parameter that is a flag rather than a quantity.

A separate class rather than a mode on `Param` so that a float
parameter still types as `float` at every use site. Flags are read as plain
attributes; `Component.si` refuses them, because converting a switch to
an SI unit is meaningless and asking for it means something is confused.

### `maiman.Port`

```python
class Port(component: Component, name: str, type: PortType) -> None
```

A reference to one named port on one component instance.

### `maiman.PortType`

- `PortType.OPTICAL`
- `PortType.ELECTRICAL`
- `PortType.BINARY`
- `PortType.SYMBOL`
- `PortType.SOFT`
- `PortType.METRIC`

What kind of signal a port carries.

Typing ports is what lets the editor reject invalid wiring at edit time
instead of failing halfway through a run. An MZM has an electrical input as
well as an optical one; without port types that distinction cannot be
expressed at all.

### `maiman.manifests`

```python
manifests() -> dict[str, dict[str, Any]]
```

Generated manifests for every registered component.

This is the component palette the GUI is built from — derived from the
classes themselves, so it cannot drift away from what the engine actually
does.

The values are `Any` rather than `object` because a manifest is a nested
structure and every real caller reaches into it: `["ports"]["inputs"]` is
the whole point of having one. Annotating the outside as `object` did not
make anything safer, it only meant nobody could read a manifest without a
cast — which is a worse guarantee than none, because the cast is where the
real mistakes get made.

### `maiman.registered_names`

```python
registered_names() -> tuple[str, ...]
```

Every registered component name, sorted.

## Signals and readings

### `maiman.OpticalSignal`

```python
class OpticalSignal(bands: tuple[Band, ...] = (), noise: tuple[NoiseBin, ...] = (), accumulated_gvd: float = 0.0, nonlinear_history: KerrHistory = <factory>, walkoff: WalkoffHistory = <factory>) -> None
```

A set of sampled bands plus the noise accompanying them.

- `band_at` — The band whose centre frequency matches `f0`.
- `delay_at` — How late the carrier at `f0` arrives [s]: see `WalkoffHistory.at`.
- `flat_noise_at` — Summed density and widest extent of the *flat* bins covering `frequency`.
- `history_at` — The `(x, y)` Kerr angle of the carrier at `f0`: see `KerrHistory.at`.
- `noise_power` — Total power in the noise bins [W].
- `noise_power_in` — ASE power inside a measurement band [W], both polarizations.
- `noise_psd_at` — One-sided ASE power spectral density at `frequency` [W/Hz per polarization].
- `shaped_noise_covering` — The shaped bins whose extent includes `frequency`.
- `signal_power` — Total power in the sampled bands [W], excluding noise bins.
- `total_power` — Signal plus noise power [W].

### `maiman.Band`

```python
class Band(Ex: np.ndarray, Ey: np.ndarray, f0: float, fs: float) -> None
```

One sampled band: the complex envelope in two orthogonal polarizations.

`Ex`/`Ey` form the Jones vector. Sample `k` of the underlying optical
field is `Ex[k] * exp(2j*pi*f0*t_k)`; the envelope is what we store.

- `average_power` — Mean power over the time window [W], summed over both polarizations.
- `bandwidth` — Sampled bandwidth [Hz], i.e. the width of the represented spectrum.
- `scale_amplitude` — Return a copy with both polarizations scaled by an *amplitude* factor.
- `wavelength` — Centre wavelength in vacuum [m].

### `maiman.NoiseBin`

```python
class NoiseBin(f_start: float, f_end: float, psd_x: float, psd_y: float, shape: NoiseShape | None = None) -> None
```

Spectrally-resolved noise power, carried outside the sampled bands.

`psd_x`/`psd_y` are one-sided power spectral densities per polarization
[W/Hz]. They are the density across `[f_start, f_end)` when the bin is
flat, and its *mean* when the bin carries a `NoiseShape` -- which is
what noise acquires by passing through a ring, an interferometer or a
grating, and what lets a density be read correctly at one frequency.

- `clip` — This bin restricted to `[start, end)` and scaled, or `None` if nothing is left.
- `density_at` — Density at one frequency [W/Hz per polarization]; zero outside the bin.
- `power_between` — Noise power this bin puts into `[low, high)` [W per polarization].
- `scale_power` — Return a copy with the PSD scaled by a *power* factor.
- `squared_density_integral` — `integral of psd**2 df` over the bin [W**2/Hz per polarization].
- `total_power` — Integrated noise power in this bin [W], both polarizations.

### `maiman.PowerReading`

```python
class PowerReading(signal_power_w: float, noise_power_w: float, bands: tuple[BandPower, ...] = ()) -> None
```

Result of a power measurement.

- `power_dbm` — Total measured power [dBm].
- `power_w` — Total measured power [W], signal plus noise.

## Circuits, netlists and PDKs

### `maiman.load_pdk`

```python
load_pdk(path: str | Path) -> PDK
```

Read a `.pdk` file. JSON in, validated `PDK` out, nothing executed.

### `maiman.load_netlist`

```python
load_netlist(path: str | Path) -> Netlist
```

Read a netlist file. JSON always; YAML when a YAML reader is installed.

JSON needs nothing — it is in the standard library, and a netlist is a plain
document. YAML is what the layout tool actually writes, and reading it needs
`PyYAML`, which is **not** a dependency of this package: one line of the
caller's own code turns a netlist into JSON, and a library that made everyone
install a parser for a file most of them will not have is the wrong trade.
When it is missing the error says so rather than reporting a syntax error in
a file that is perfectly valid.

### `maiman.circuit_from_netlist`

```python
circuit_from_netlist(netlist: Netlist, pdk: PDK, frequencies: Sequence[float] | np.ndarray, *, wavelength: float | None = None, polarization: str = te) -> Circuit
```

Build the circuit a netlist describes, with a kit's numbers in it.

Returns an unsolved `maiman.circuit.Circuit` rather than its matrix,
because the caller may want to add to it — a source, a facet, a device the
layout does not carry — and because a function that both assembles and solves
gives no place to stand in between when the answer looks wrong.

`wavelength` evaluates the kit's fits somewhere other than its reference,
the same way `PDK.make` does. It is *not* the grid: the models here are
frequency-flat by construction and a fit is resolved once, at build time, so
a C-band sweep of a kit fitted at 1550 uses the 1550 numbers across the sweep
unless told otherwise. Sweeping the fit itself means building the circuit
again at each wavelength, which is a loop the caller writes and can see.

## Errors

### `maiman.GraphError`

Invalid graph structure, detected before any component runs.

### `maiman.CycleError`

The graph contains a feedback loop with no loop-control component.

Cycles are not forbidden in principle — recirculating loops and optical
feedback are real — but they need an explicit component that declares how
many times the loop runs -- `maiman.components.Feedback`. Leaving the
semantics implicit would make results
depend on scheduler internals.

### `maiman.ProjectError`

A project file could not be read.

### `maiman.UnknownComponentError`

A project file names a component that nothing has registered.
